paragraphs: WaveGC addresses how neural networks filter information on graphs at different spatial scales. Spectral graph convolution depends on both a representation for transforming graph signals and a filter that acts on that representation. The paper argues that commonly used Fourier representations and vector-valued filters restrict flexibility when signals contain information spread across large regions.

The proposed network combines wavelet representations at multiple resolutions with a matrix-valued filter. This gives the model a richer way to handle information at different scales. The theoretical analysis establishes that WaveGC can capture and separate short-range and long-range information, supporting more flexible filtering than existing graph wavelet neural networks.

To construct the wavelets, the authors combine odd and even Chebyshev polynomial terms separately. This construction satisfies the mathematical admissibility requirements for wavelets. Numerical experiments report consistent improvements on tasks involving both nearby and distant graph information. Together, the theory and experiments support the value of designing the signal representation and filtering mechanism jointly.
icml-2025-a-general-graph-spectral-wavel.tldr: WaveGC combines multiresolution graph wavelets with matrix-valued filters to better separate and use short-range and long-range information.

paragraphs: A unified neural vehicle-routing solver must handle several kinds of routing problems using one model. The paper identifies a possible weakness in existing approaches: different tasks can have different underlying geometric structures, yet their representations may not account for those differences. Ignoring that structure can lead to poorer solutions even when the solver works across multiple tasks.

The authors propose curvature-aware pre-training, introducing mixed-curvature spaces at the stage where features are combined. Rather than treating all instances as having the same geometry, this representation encourages the model to capture geometric properties associated with each instance. The contribution is a pre-training strategy evaluated with existing multi-task solvers.

Experiments cover multiple testing scenarios and report better generalization on synthetic datasets, alongside improved solution quality on real-world benchmarks. These findings suggest that geometry-aware representations can benefit both transfer across generated routing instances and performance on practical routing data. The stated result concerns improvements to existing solvers through pre-training, with the feature-fusion stage providing the central mechanism.
icml-2025-a-mixed-curvature-based-pre-tr.tldr: Curvature-aware pre-training improves multi-task vehicle-routing solvers by incorporating instance geometry when combining features.

paragraphs: Classifying nodes in a changing graph becomes harder when new classes appear and existing classes also evolve. Training again on all available data is expensive, while learning only the new classes can erase earlier knowledge. The paper argues that retaining small samples of old classes is insufficient if those samples do not account for how the classes change over time.

The authors formulate temporal graph continual learning around maintaining current knowledge of old classes efficiently. Their framework, Learning Towards the Future, replaces the full old-class data with selected subsets. They derive an upper bound on the error introduced by this replacement and use it to guide both subset selection and learning.

The resulting objectives balance classification accuracy with preserving the distribution represented by the complete old-class data. Experiments on three real-world datasets show that the framework addresses this evolving-class setting effectively. Its contribution is to connect economical data retention with keeping old knowledge up to date, so remembering a class also accounts for its subsequent evolution.
icml-2025-a-selective-learning-method-fo.tldr: Learning Towards the Future selects representative data subsets to maintain knowledge of evolving old classes as new graph classes arrive.

paragraphs: Language models used for decision-making need judgments that remain coherent across related questions. A model can produce individually plausible preferences that contradict one another when considered together. This paper studies logical preference consistency as a foundation for more dependable decisions and develops a framework for measuring it across models.

The framework evaluates three properties: transitivity, commutativity, and negation invariance. These examine whether preferences maintain the logical relationships expected across linked comparisons and changes in how comparisons are expressed. Experiments across diverse language models find that these properties are strong indicators of judgment robustness, giving the evaluation a connection to practical reliability.

The authors also introduce REPAIR, a technique that refines and augments training data to improve consistency while maintaining alignment with human preferences. They report that greater consistency improves performance in logic-based algorithms driven by language models. This connects the measurement framework to an intervention and a downstream benefit: more coherent component judgments can make the algorithms using those judgments work better.
icml-2025-aligning-with-logic-measuring-.tldr: The paper measures logical consistency in model preferences and introduces REPAIR to improve it while preserving human-preference alignment.

paragraphs: Graphical causal analysis can involve counting the directed acyclic graphs represented by a single Markov equivalence class. The input here is a completed partially directed acyclic graph, which represents that class. An existing polynomial-time method, Clique-Picking, performs the count by considering different root cliques and working through the orientations and unresolved components each choice produces.

The paper targets the repeated generation of unresolved undirected connected components. Changing the root clique changes the calculation, but previously computed results can still be useful. The authors introduce super cliques inside rooted clique trees and show how to transfer them efficiently between trees with different roots.

This reuse reduces the computational complexity of the original method. The improvement is especially relevant when the graph has substantially fewer cliques than vertices and edges, a structural qualification emphasized in the abstract. The contribution therefore makes an established counting procedure more efficient by carrying useful intermediate structure between related computations, rather than rebuilding each root-dependent calculation independently.
icml-2025-an-improved-clique-picking-alg.tldr: Transferring super-clique information between rooted clique trees reduces repeated work when counting Markov-equivalent directed acyclic graphs.

paragraphs: Continual reinforcement learning asks an agent to learn a sequence of tasks without losing its ability to perform earlier ones. This paper tackles forgetting through a model of world dynamics that is updated online. The agent uses that model to plan actions for tasks described by reward functions.

The proposed Online Agent learns a shallow world model using Follow-The-Leader and plans with model predictive control. Its action search always uses the latest model, allowing the agent to update incrementally. The authors describe the world model as immune to forgetting by construction and establish a regret bound under mild assumptions. That theoretical claim is tied to the proposed construction and its assumptions.

For evaluation, the authors introduce Continual Bench and compare agents within the same model-planning framework. Their agent learns new tasks while retaining old skills in the reported experiments, outperforming agents that combine deep world models with various continual-learning techniques. The findings support online dynamics learning plus planning as an approach to maintaining capabilities across sequential tasks.
icml-2025-continual-reinforcement-learni.tldr: An incrementally learned shallow world model enables planning across sequential tasks while retaining earlier skills in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Robot control benefits from large training datasets, but collecting realistic robot experience is costly. Simulation offers faster and cheaper data generation at scale, yet differences between virtual and physical environments can make the resulting skills difficult to deploy. DexScale addresses this problem by automating the creation and expansion of simulated manipulation data.

The data engine incorporates diverse forms of realistic data into simulated environments to keep the generated skills aligned with the intended tasks. For each skill, it automates domain randomization and adaptation. These steps connect data scaling with the transfer problem: producing more simulated experience is paired with making that experience useful outside the simulator.

Policies tuned using the scaled dataset achieve zero-shot transfer from simulation to reality in the reported evaluations. The results span diverse tasks, multiple robot embodiments, and widely studied policy architectures. This breadth supports the usefulness of the data-generation process across several control settings. The central finding is that automated scaling, combined with realistic task alignment and adaptation, can produce training data that supports deployable manipulation policies.
icml-2025-dexscale-automating-data-scali.tldr: DexScale automates realistic simulation-data generation and scaling to support zero-shot robot-policy transfer across tested tasks and embodiments.

paragraphs: Estimating a vehicle's drag coefficient helps assess aerodynamic performance, fuel consumption, and energy efficiency. Conventional fluid simulations and wind-tunnel tests are costly for rapidly changing designs. DragSolver uses a Transformer to estimate drag directly from large, diverse three-dimensional vehicle models, targeting the complexity of real automotive geometry.

The framework combines several mechanisms. Multiscale feature extraction captures overall shape and fine geometric detail, while scale normalization handles meshes with different sizes and densities. Surface-guided gating suppresses internal structures that are irrelevant to external aerodynamics. Monte Carlo dropout provides estimates of epistemic uncertainty, allowing the prediction process to account for uncertainty in the model's knowledge.

Evaluations on DrivaerNet, DrivaerNet++, and DrivaerML report better accuracy and generalization than existing approaches, including a 58.7% average reduction in relative L2 error across real-world datasets. The authors also report the first reliable real-time drag-coefficient inference on production-level automotive geometries. These findings connect the architectural choices to both prediction quality and the speed needed for iterative vehicle design.
icml-2025-dragsolver-a-multi-scale-trans.tldr: DragSolver estimates automotive drag from detailed 3D geometry, reporting real-time inference and a 58.7% average reduction in relative L2 error.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how far language-model architectures can go in image generation through careful design choices. The authors argue that existing approaches either introduce specialized visual designs or leave the potential of language models insufficiently explored. Their study examines how images are represented and generated within the language-model framework.

The investigation covers tokenization, modeling approaches, scan patterns, vocabulary design, and sampling strategies. These choices determine how image information becomes a sequence and how the model produces that sequence. The authors also study learning and scaling behavior, finding that larger autoregressive models capture more useful information than smaller ones. They examine differences between text and images to inform applications across domains.

The resulting model, ELM, achieves an FID of 1.54 on 256-by-256 ImageNet and 3.29 on 512-by-512 ImageNet. The abstract characterizes the performance as near state of the art without domain-specific designs. The main implication is that choosing the representation and generation procedure carefully can make a general language-model approach highly competitive for image synthesis.
icml-2025-elucidating-the-design-space-o.tldr: A systematic study of image representation and generation choices yields near-state-of-the-art image synthesis with language models lacking domain-specific designs.

paragraphs: Federated graph learning distributes portions of a graph across devices that cannot directly share raw data. Splitting the graph can remove links between those portions, weakening node representations. Existing approaches can also depend heavily on labeled examples. FedNCN addresses these issues through node clustering and restoration of cross-subgraph relationships.

Each client uses an MLP-based projector to preserve important clustering properties through a denoising-like learning process. It uploads clustering signals described as difficult to reconstruct. The server estimates graph similarity from these signals to identify potential relationships between subgraphs, then uses the normalized-cut criterion to reduce redundant links.

A graph neural network learns shared consensus prototypes from the repaired graph. Joint optimization of the MLP and graph network then supports better local clustering and enhances privacy during transmission, according to the abstract. Extensive experiments report superior performance. The method's central idea is to use clustering structure as a shared basis for recovering relationships lost during graph partitioning while keeping the original data local.
icml-2025-federated-node-level-clusterin.tldr: FedNCN shares clustering signals to repair missing cross-device graph links and improve local node clustering while keeping raw data local.

paragraphs: Stochastic interpolants provide a framework for generative models that transform one data distribution into another using differential equations. Earlier analyses largely considered continuous time and assumed those equations could be solved perfectly. Actual sampling requires discrete computational steps, so understanding the resulting error is important for connecting the framework to an implementable procedure.

The paper introduces a discrete-time sampler and derives an upper bound on its distribution-estimation error after a finite amount of computation. The analysis quantifies how factors including the distance between source and target distributions and the accuracy of estimation affect convergence. This gives a structured account of what influences how quickly the sampler approaches its target.

The result also motivates a principled way to choose sampling schedules that accelerate convergence. Numerical experiments with the proposed sampler corroborate the theoretical findings. The contribution links finite-step sampling, error control, and schedule design within the stochastic-interpolant framework, extending the analysis beyond idealized continuous-time solutions.
icml-2025-finite-time-analysis-of-discre.tldr: A discrete-time stochastic-interpolant sampler comes with finite-time error bounds that explain convergence factors and guide faster sampling schedules.

paragraphs: In-context learning uses demonstration examples to help a language model perform a task. Selecting useful examples and processing many of them can require substantial effort and time. This paper explores an approach centered on the model's internal activations, asking whether those representations can be adjusted during inference to improve in-context performance.

The proposed technique, Iterative Vectors, extracts activation-based meta-gradients and refines them repeatedly. It applies these signals during inference to simulate gradient updates without using backpropagation at any stage. The key mechanism is an iterative search through activation space: internal steering signals are developed and applied as the model performs the task.

Evaluations across various tasks using four popular models show significant improvements in the reported experiments. The findings support activation steering as a promising direction for enhancing in-context learning. In particular, they indicate that useful iterative adjustment can occur during inference through activation-based signals, expanding the ways a model can use task information beyond the direct processing of demonstrations.
icml-2025-iterative-vectors-in-context-g.tldr: Iterative Vectors improve in-context performance by repeatedly refining activation-based steering signals during inference without backpropagation.

paragraphs: A model's ability to finish a passage exactly is often used as evidence that the passage appeared in training. Interpreting that test requires a definition of training-set membership. This paper examines definitions based on n-gram overlap, which assess membership using matching sequences of a chosen length between the target and training data.

The authors find cases where completion succeeds even though the target is a non-member under the selected definition. They retrain models from scratch after removing training samples that had been completed and identify natural cases involving duplicates, near-duplicates, and short overlaps. These observations make it difficult to select one overlap length that yields a consistently useful membership definition.

Using those insights, the authors construct adversarial datasets that cause a target sequence to be completed without containing it under any reasonable chosen n. The findings challenge the adequacy of overlap-based membership and its interpretation through completion tests. Their explanation emphasizes auxiliary information available during training, which can support exact completion without the target satisfying the chosen membership rule.
icml-2025-language-models-may-verbatim-c.tldr: Exact text completion can succeed for sequences classified as absent by n-gram membership rules, exposing weaknesses in those definitions.

paragraphs: Continuous-control reinforcement learning can require extensive interaction with an environment. Demonstrations can help start training, but both demonstrations and subsequently collected experience may be imperfect. The paper identifies a weakness in methods that evaluate each action dimension independently: they overlook dependencies that matter when identifying good combined actions from suboptimal data.

Auto-Regressive Soft Q-learning addresses this through a coarse-to-fine representation of actions and sequential prediction within each decision. It divides continuous action spaces into a hierarchy of discrete spaces, supporting progressively finer control. Within a decision step, it predicts action advantages autoregressively, allowing decisions across action dimensions to reflect their interdependencies.

The authors evaluate the method on D4RL and RLBench while incorporating demonstrations into online training. On D4RL, which includes non-expert demonstrations, they report an average 1.62-fold performance improvement over a state-of-the-art value-based baseline. On RLBench, where demonstrations are expert-provided, the method surpasses several baselines. Those results also support its ability to learn from imperfect experience collected during online training.
icml-2025-learning-from-suboptimal-data-.tldr: ARSQ combines coarse-to-fine action choices with autoregressive value modeling to improve continuous control learned from imperfect experience.

paragraphs: Neural processes support transfer across tasks by learning with distributions of functions. Their ability to adapt quickly can vary substantially between tasks, making poor adaptation especially concerning in risk-sensitive settings. This paper changes the training objective to control bad adaptation outcomes at a specified probabilistic level.

The authors reformulate risk-averse training as a two-level finite-sum minimax optimization problem. They solve it using a double-loop stochastic mirror-prox algorithm with task-aware variance reduction, drawing samples across tasks. Mirror prox supports complex constraints and non-Euclidean geometries. The final output combines intermediate prox points using adaptive learning rates to promote stability and solution quality.

The training strategy can be applied to various neural processes and has a theoretical guarantee for a less biased approximation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data report improvements in both accuracy and robustness. The contribution connects a probabilistic concern about poor adaptation with a concrete optimization procedure, making the distribution of outcomes across tasks an explicit part of model training.
icml-2025-learning-robust-neural-process.tldr: Risk-averse training improves neural-process accuracy and robustness by explicitly controlling poor fast-adaptation outcomes at a probabilistic level.

paragraphs: A Transformer's highest-ranked prediction can stop changing before computation reaches the final layer. This paper asks what later layers do after that saturation event. The authors extend the analysis to several top-ranked tokens and observe similar stabilization events in language, vision, and speech models.

The reported pattern follows token rank: the highest-ranked token stabilizes first, followed by the second, then later-ranked tokens. It appears across Transformer variants and even in untrained models, suggesting that the architecture itself may contribute. The authors propose that these events mark transitions between discrete tasks, with each task determining another position in the ranking.

They support this interpretation by predicting the current task from hidden-layer embeddings and intervening to move the model to the next task. They also introduce a token-level early-exit strategy that improves the performance-efficiency balance over existing methods and use saturation events to improve language modeling. The findings give later-layer computation a more detailed interpretation than simply refining the single most likely output.
icml-2025-looking-beyond-the-top-1-trans.tldr: Transformer token rankings stabilize in rank order, a finding the authors use to interpret later layers and improve inference efficiency.

paragraphs: Asking a model to reason step by step often improves performance, but the effect depends on the task. This paper investigates settings where chain-of-thought reasoning can make results worse. It takes inspiration from cognitive psychology, selecting six representative tasks where deliberate thinking has been found to harm human performance.

On three of those tasks, the evaluated state-of-the-art models show significant performance declines with chain of thought. The abstract reports a drop of up to 36.3 percentage points in accuracy for OpenAI o1-preview compared with GPT-4o. On the remaining tasks, the effects vary, including improvements, little change, and declines. The reported pattern therefore does not support treating deliberation as uniformly helpful or harmful.

The authors emphasize that model and human cognitive processes are not perfectly parallel. Their contribution is to use known human difficulties as a guide for locating model failures. Connecting psychological findings with model evaluations offers a way to study when additional inference-time reasoning helps and when it can interfere with successful task performance.
icml-2025-mind-your-step-by-step-chain-o.tldr: Tasks where deliberation harms humans help identify cases where chain-of-thought reasoning also reduces model performance, although effects vary.

paragraphs: Multilayer matrix factorization generalizes classic matrix factorization and may offer a more expressive model. This paper studies its probabilistic formulation, where a central challenge is finding an inference procedure that is both computationally efficient and accurate. The authors focus on variational inference as a way to approximate maximum-likelihood inference.

A variational autoencoder is one established approach, using neural networks to define the variational process. The proposed method instead draws inspiration from variational diffusion models developed for generation. It introduces a diffusion process that reduces dimension, creating a different way for the inference procedure to interact with the factorization model's layered structure.

Experiments show improved performance scores over several existing approaches, including the variational autoencoder. These results support dimension-reducing diffusion as a useful variational mechanism for multilayer matrix factorization. The contribution concerns how inference is organized within the probabilistic model: it connects diffusion-based inference ideas to the layered structure of factorization and demonstrates empirical benefits from that connection.
icml-2025-multilayer-matrix-factorizatio.tldr: A dimension-reducing diffusion process improves variational inference for probabilistic multilayer matrix factorization in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Combinatorial bandit problems involve decisions made from combinations of components. Most existing work learns through online interaction, which can be costly even when historical datasets are already available. Off-CMAB develops an offline framework for learning such decisions from existing data, avoiding the need to frame learning entirely around new interactions.

Its central algorithm, combinatorial lower confidence bound, combines pessimistic reward estimates with combinatorial solvers. The authors introduce two data-coverage conditions to describe when an offline dataset supplies sufficient information. Under those conditions, they prove a near-optimal suboptimality gap, matching the theoretical lower bound up to a logarithmic factor.

Applications include ranking, language-model caching, and social influence maximization. The framework handles nonlinear rewards, general feedback, and demonstrated settings where logged actions exclude optimal or even feasible actions. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report superior performance. The result connects practical use of imperfect historical data with a conditional theoretical account of how dataset coverage supports good combinatorial decisions.
icml-2025-offline-learning-for-combinato.tldr: Off-CMAB learns combinatorial decisions from offline data, with near-optimal guarantees under proposed coverage conditions and strong reported empirical performance.

paragraphs: Predicting protein-ligand binding energy is useful for drug discovery, but supervised learning depends on labeled examples that can be scarce. CEBind uses unlabeled protein-ligand complexes by deriving a learning relationship from conservation of energy. This gives the model a physically grounded constraint for comparing related configurations.

Starting with a complex, the method samples forces for atoms in the ligand. It applies those forces to move the ligand as a rigid body, following rigid-body dynamics. The model predicts energies for the original and perturbed complexes. Conservation of energy links the difference between those predictions to the work performed by the applied external forces.

This construction turns controlled perturbations into a source of training information without requiring binding-energy labels for the complexes. Experiments on unsupervised binding-energy prediction benchmarks, together with theoretical analysis, support improved efficiency and performance over previous unsupervised models. The approach matters because it uses a known physical relationship to constrain predictions where direct labeled supervision is difficult to obtain.
icml-2025-physics-aware-neural-networks-.tldr: CEBind learns binding-energy predictions from unlabeled complexes by linking rigid ligand perturbations to energy changes through conservation of energy.

paragraphs: Sparsification replaces a graph with a smaller representation that approximately preserves properties needed by later algorithms. Hypergraph sparsification extends this idea to structures whose edges can connect groups of vertices. The paper presents a quantum algorithm for this problem, addressing an open question about whether quantum computation can accelerate it.

For a weighted hypergraph with n vertices, m hyperedges, and rank r, the algorithm produces a near-linear-size epsilon-spectral sparsifier. Its running time is Õ(r√(mn)/epsilon), where the notation suppresses logarithmic factors. The authors compare this with the state-of-the-art classical time of Õ(mr) and establish a quantum speedup. For constant rank, the algorithm matches the quantum lower bound.

The paper also derives speedups for constructing hypergraph cut sparsifiers and approximating minimum cuts, including cuts separating designated source and target vertices. These applications show why the sparsification result matters beyond compression alone: a faster structure-preserving reduction can accelerate additional hypergraph computations. The constant-rank condition specifically qualifies the claim of matching the quantum lower bound.
icml-2025-quantum-speedup-for-hypergraph.tldr: A quantum hypergraph-sparsification algorithm achieves a speedup over the cited classical method and matches the quantum lower bound for constant rank.

paragraphs: Real-time rendering increasingly uses neural networks to improve images through denoising, supersampling, and frame extrapolation. These workloads must balance visual quality with tight frame-time requirements. Because consecutive frames share information, some intermediate neural computations can potentially be reused instead of repeated for every frame.

ReFrame applies layer caching to this setting, extending an idea previously shown useful for diffusion-model inference. It investigates different caching policies to manage the trade-off between reusing intermediate features and preserving output quality. The approach applies to a variety of encoder-decoder networks commonly used in rendering pipelines, making the caching decision relevant across several rendering workloads.

Across three real-time rendering tasks, the experiments report an average 1.4-fold speedup with negligible quality loss. The result indicates that temporal coherence can provide computational savings inside the neural network itself. Its practical significance lies in using similarities between successive frames to reduce inference latency while retaining the image quality expected from the underlying rendering task.
icml-2025-reframe-layer-caching-for-acce.tldr: ReFrame reuses intermediate neural features across rendered frames, achieving an average 1.4-fold speedup with negligible quality loss in three tasks.

paragraphs: Low-Rank Adaptation makes large-model fine-tuning more memory-efficient, but its performance can fall behind full fine-tuning, particularly on difficult reasoning and coding tasks. SeedLoRA investigates whether multiple adaptations of the same task can be combined to improve results. Its starting observation is that different random seeds often produce models with complementary strengths.

The approach fuses LoRA models trained on the same task using different seeds. This makes variation between training runs the source of diversity being combined. The aim is to obtain a more robust and effective adaptation by bringing together strengths that are distributed across those individually fine-tuned models.

Experiments cover mathematical reasoning, code generation, and general instruction tuning. The reported fusion method significantly improves performance over standalone LoRA models and existing fusion methods, substantially narrowing the gap to full fine-tuning. The findings suggest that variation between same-task training runs can be useful for improving adaptation while avoiding the GPU-memory burden associated with updating every model parameter.
icml-2025-seedlora-a-fusion-approach-to-.tldr: SeedLoRA fuses same-task LoRA models trained with different random seeds to improve performance and narrow the gap to full fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Generating a song from text requires coordinating vocals and accompaniment while respecting musical instructions. Existing multistage approaches can create complicated training and inference pipelines, with errors accumulating between stages. SongGen uses a single autoregressive Transformer framework to support controllable song generation within one stage.

Users can specify lyrics and descriptions of instrumentation, genre, mood, and timbre. An optional three-second reference clip supports voice cloning. The framework offers two output modes: one directly produces vocals mixed with accompaniment, while the other generates separate vocal and accompaniment tracks. Separate tracks provide additional flexibility for downstream uses.

The authors investigate different token patterns for both modes and report notable improvements from those choices. They also develop an automated preprocessing pipeline with quality control to support the data preparation needed for training. The abstract describes SongGen as open source, provides available code, and states plans to release weights, training code, annotated data, and the preprocessing pipeline. The contribution combines generation control, alternative output formats, and a unified training approach.
icml-2025-songgen-a-single-stage-auto-re.tldr: SongGen uses one autoregressive Transformer to generate controllable songs as mixed audio or separate vocal and accompaniment tracks.

paragraphs: Time to first token measures how long a user waits before a language model starts responding. Processing the prompt can be compute-bound, with the bottleneck shifting from attention to the model's MLP components. SpecPrefill targets this initial processing cost for medium and long contexts through selective use of prompt tokens.

A lightweight model estimates which tokens are locally important given the context. It passes the selected tokens, together with necessary positional information, to the main model. The framework requires no training and rests on the insight that a carefully chosen prompt subset can preserve output quality. Reducing the amount of prompt material processed by the main model is the central acceleration mechanism.

The authors evaluate diverse tasks, end-to-end serving performance, and component choices through ablations. For Llama-3.1-405B-Instruct-FP8, they report up to sevenfold maximal end-to-end query throughput on real downstream tasks and a 7.66-fold improvement in time to first token. These are reported performance gains for the evaluated system, illustrating the potential value of lightweight token selection before expensive prompt processing.
icml-2025-speculative-prefill-turbocharg.tldr: SpecPrefill uses a lightweight model to select important prompt tokens, reporting up to sevenfold throughput and 7.66-fold time-to-first-token improvements.
